implementation_notes: JavaScript has no lazy modifier, but deferral is idiomatic: a getter that computes on first read and caches (MDN documents the smart or self-overwriting getter, which deletes itself and re-adds the value as a data property), or a private field initialized with `this.#res ??= acquire()` because ??= evaluates its right-hand side only when the left side is still nullish. Module-level acquisition is deferred by the language itself: import() loads and evaluates a module on demand and the module namespace object is cached, so a second import() of the same specifier returns the same instance without re-running it. A realm runs one thread at a time, so the guard cannot tear between bytecodes - but two awaits can interleave, so an asynchronous lazy accessor must memoize the in-flight promise rather than the resolved value.
pitfalls: ??= caches only non-nullish results, and ||= only truthy ones: if acquisition legitimately produces null, undefined, 0 or "", every access re-acquires - use a sentinel object or a separate boolean flag.
An async lazy accessor that caches the resolved value re-acquires when two callers await before the first promise settles; memoize the promise instead (this.#pending ??= openAsync()).

Self-overwriting getters call delete on the accessor: on a non-configurable property (Object.freeze, or defineProperty with configurable: false) that throws in strict mode or silently fails, and the value is recomputed on every read.
A dynamic import never re-evaluates a module - failures during evaluation are cached - so retryable acquisition belongs in an exported function, never in module top-level code.
